claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy is a single-phase hexagonal material.
The as-deposited alloy has high intrinsic residual stress.
Residual stress in the as-deposited alloy produces a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition with a large, hysteretic entropy change.
Annealing near 300°C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere will relieve residual stress.
The proposed annealing treatment will induce subtle nanoscale ordering.
Annealing near 300°C for 1 hour will avoid significant grain coarsening and phase separation.
Keeping annealing below approximately 350°C and 2 hours will avoid unintended phase changes and loss of mechanical stability.
Residual-stress reduction and nanoscale ordering modify local energy landscapes at phase boundaries.
Lattice or structural changes can modify magnetic exchange interactions and magnetocaloric behavior.
Annealing lowers the distribution of energy barriers governing the magnetostructural transition.
Stress relief and nanoscale ordering reduce magnetic-domain pinning under low applied fields.
Reduced energy barriers and domain pinning will broaden the transition-temperature interval and reduce magnetic hysteresis.
Relative to the as-deposited state, the annealed alloy will have a broader magnetocaloric temperature range.
Relative to the as-deposited state, the annealed alloy will have lower hysteresis during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Annealing may slightly decrease the peak magnetic entropy change.
Broadening the entropy-change peak can improve overall refrigerant capacity even if the peak entropy change decreases.
The as-deposited material has a low surface-to-volume ratio that limits heat exchange.
The annealed alloy will have better heat-exchange characteristics than the as-deposited baseline.
The predictions apply only while annealing remains below the regime causing grain growth or phase separation.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says annealing lowers the distribution of transition-energy barriers but then attributes a broader transition-temperature distribution to that change; the hypothesis does not reconcile why a reduced barrier distribution would broaden rather than narrow the transition.

Limited heat exchange is attributed to low surface-to-volume ratio, but the annealing intervention does not change sample geometry and is explicitly intended to avoid major grain-size changes, so the predicted improvement in heat exchange does not follow from the stated intervention.
